## Pre-race

This race had a slightly odd place in my season.

On paper, it was not the biggest target. It was not a world qualifier, and by
late August I was already at the point where the main work of the season was
done. But it still mattered to me for two reasons.

First, I wanted to finish the year properly. Second, there were still useful
points available for the MultiSport Canada duathlon series. So even if this was
more of a `B` race than an `A` race, I still wanted to race it well.

I had also been here before, two years earlier, for the sprint triathlon. I did
not enjoy that version of the event at all. The swim had one of those awkward
long entries and exits through shallow water where it is too deep to run well
and too shallow to swim properly.

Still, a duathlon is a different story. No swim, no awkward water entry, and a
course format that at least gave me a reason to give the place another chance.

There was also a bit of self-imposed pressure in the background. Two years ago
I finished `5th` overall here, albeit in a different event. And coming into
this race I had already raced three times this season and finished `2nd`,
`2nd`, and `3rd`. So the question in my head was fairly simple: could I make it
four podiums from four starts?

## A Better Build-up

Compared with the build-up to Barrie, this one was much more normal.

That may sound like a low bar, but after the ER visit and the blood pressure
medication drama earlier in the month, "normal" was a meaningful upgrade.
Training was not perfect, but it was uninterrupted, and I came into the race
feeling more like an athlete preparing for a race and less like someone trying
to improvise their way through damage control.

I still would not say I felt especially sharp. It was late in the season, and
there is a difference between being healthy enough to race and being truly
primed to race. But I was in a much better place than I had been three weeks
earlier.

That changed the goal a bit. In Barrie, the first objective was just to race
safely and get around. Here, the objective was to race properly.

![](https://storage.googleapis.com/blogs_josa/sport/blog_assets/2026-08-29_WASAGA_BEACH_SPRINT_DUATHLON/img/thumbnail/00b.jpg)

## Race morning

The warm-up was fine, but not especially inspiring.

I felt a bit sluggish, and the main thing I noticed was some tightness in the
back of the legs. Not full cramping, not quite panic-inducing, but enough to
put the thought in my head that this might become relevant later.

On the start line I noticed a few guys who looked strong, plus Michael Shay,
who had finished behind me in Barrie and ended up `3rd` in our category there.
He had been almost six minutes behind me that day, but that does not mean much:
you never know if somebody else is also going through a rough patch in their preparation.

There were also a bunch of under-19 athletes at the front who started with the
kind of enthusiasm that usually means one of two things: either they are very
good, or they are about to have a difficult second half of the race.

[![](https://storage.googleapis.com/blogs_josa/sport/blog_assets/2026-08-29_WASAGA_BEACH_SPRINT_DUATHLON/img/thumbnail/07.jpg)](https://storage.googleapis.com/blogs_josa/sport/blog_assets/2026-08-29_WASAGA_BEACH_SPRINT_DUATHLON/img/full/07.jpg)

## Run 1

I started, as usual, with the intention of being sensible.

Also as usual, that intention lasted about five seconds.

The plan had been to keep things around `4:20/km` early on and then reassess.
Instead, the first look at the watch showed something like `3:45/km`. After
that it settled more into the `4:05` to `4:10/km` range, but by then the damage
was already being negotiated rather than avoided.

Michael and I ran together for roughly the first half of the opening `5K`.
Then he started to drift away. I could tell that matching him would cost me too
much, so I let him go and focused on running my own race, confident that I had
good biking legs.

The closing part of the run was harder. The pace started to slip, more toward
the `4:25` to `4:35/km` range, and I was already asking myself the familiar
question of whether I will ever learn how not to overcook the first run of a
duathlon.

Even so, the damage was manageable. The final results show that I had the `3rd` fastest
run in my category and `9th` overall, which kept me very much in the race. But I did
not know that at the time, in part because it was a wave start.


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

activities_metadata <- read.csv(
  "analysis_data/activities_metadata.csv",
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

activities_data <- read.csv(
  "analysis_data/activities_data.csv",
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  na.strings = c("NA", "")
)

run_1_id <- activities_metadata |>
  filter(EVENT_TYPE == "RUN") |>
  distinct(ID) |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(ID)

run_1_plot_data <- activities_data |>
  filter(ID == run_1_id) |>
  transmute(
    time_min = as.numeric(SECS) / 60,
    pace_min_km = as.numeric(PACE),
    power_w = na_if(as.numeric(WATTS), 0),
    cadence_spm = na_if(as.numeric(CAD), 0),
    hr_bpm = na_if(as.numeric(HR), 0)
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(pace_min_km, power_w, cadence_spm, hr_bpm),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric = factor(
      metric,
      levels = c("pace_min_km", "power_w", "cadence_spm", "hr_bpm"),
      labels = c("Pace [min/km]", "Power [W]", "Cadence [spm]", "HR [bpm]")
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(value))

format_pace <- function(pace_min_km) {
  total_seconds <- round(pace_min_km * 60)
  minutes <- total_seconds %/% 60
  seconds <- total_seconds %% 60
  sprintf("%d:%02d/km", minutes, seconds)
}

run_1_average_table <- run_1_plot_data |>
  mutate(
    period = case_when(
      time_min >= 5 & time_min < 14 ~ "Before breaking point",
      time_min >= 14 ~ "After breaking point",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(period)) |>
  group_by(metric, period) |>
  summarise(value = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    value = case_when(
      metric == "Pace [min/km]" ~ format_pace(value),
      TRUE ~ as.character(round(value))
    )
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = value) |>
  select(metric, `Before breaking point`, `After breaking point`) |>
  rename(Metric = metric)

ggplot(run_1_plot_data, aes(x = time_min, y = value)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5, color = "#1f4e79") +
  #geom_vline(xintercept = 14, color = "red", linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Time [min]",
    y = NULL,
    title = "Run 1 performance review"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

This time there was no clear drop, except for run cadence after `15 min`.
Rather, there was a constant decline. This was caused by a lack of race fitness,
but also by me trying to control the pace.
The drop in cadence is a bit concerning; I'll need to work on that.

## T1

This time, at least, transition did not turn into a comedy routine.

Two years prior in Wasaga I lost over a minute hunting for my bib number like
an idiot. Here, T1 was much cleaner. I still had the usual small struggle
getting my feet into the shoes, but only the left one caused any real trouble,
so by my standards that counts as efficient.

The numbers back that up. I had the fastest `T1` in my category and the `2nd`
fastest overall, which moved me from `3rd` to `2nd` in the `Men40-49` race. Again,
I did not know this at the time, and this will come into play later.

## Bike

[![](https://storage.googleapis.com/blogs_josa/sport/blog_assets/2026-08-29_WASAGA_BEACH_SPRINT_DUATHLON/img/thumbnail/17.jpg)](https://storage.googleapis.com/blogs_josa/sport/blog_assets/2026-08-29_WASAGA_BEACH_SPRINT_DUATHLON/img/full/17.jpg)

Once onto the bike, the race settled down.

This is normally the leg where I feel most in control, and that was true again
here. The goal was straightforward: ride strongly, reel in anyone available to
reel in, and build enough of a gap that the final `2.5K` would become a matter
of managing the advantage rather than trying to create it from scratch.

What made the bike leg slightly confusing was that I did not have a great read
on where my direct competition actually was.

By the turnaround, I still had not seen another obvious rider from my category
ahead of me. Before I reached the turnaround, I saw one of the duathletes in my
category, too far ahead for me to catch, and a few of the younger guys
who had gone out hard on the first run, but I had not seen Michael Shay, which
was concerning. With only about `10K` left at that point, every minute matters,
and I did not feel as though I had created much separation.

Then, shortly after the turnaround, I saw him behind me.

That was a surprise, because I am fairly sure I had not passed him on the road.
The most likely explanation is that I got him in transition, which would also
fit with what happened in Barrie, and the Sportstats numbers confirm this.
Either way, it clarified the race. I knew I had someone I needed to stay ahead of,
 and I knew the margin was not large enough to relax.

So I pressed a bit more.

I wanted at least `20` seconds, ideally more. In the end I came off the bike
`2nd` in category and `3rd` overall, with a `1:38` advantage over Michael
Shay and still with a real shot at the podium. I will repeat myself, but I did
not know any of this. In my head Michael was just a few seconds behind me.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

bike_plot_data <- activities_data |>

ggplot(bike_plot_data, aes(x = time_min, y = value)) +

```

The data is telling us that it was a very even ride. Not too hard,
as the HR went down from the run, and pretty consistent. If only I could run in the
same way...

## T2

T2 was uneventful, which is exactly what you want.

I got through cleanly, albeit a bit slowly, and started the final run still
`2nd` in category. At
that point the race had become very simple: hold the place if possible, and at
the very least make anyone who wanted it work very hard for it.

## Run 2

[![](https://storage.googleapis.com/blogs_josa/sport/blog_assets/2026-08-29_WASAGA_BEACH_SPRINT_DUATHLON/img/thumbnail/18.jpg)](https://storage.googleapis.com/blogs_josa/sport/blog_assets/2026-08-29_WASAGA_BEACH_SPRINT_DUATHLON/img/full/18.jpg)


From the start of the second run, I knew this was going to hurt.

I could feel the lower legs threatening to cramp, and that made the whole thing
more tactical than heroic. The effort was hard, but it also had to stay just
controlled enough that the legs did not fully lock up.

At the same time, I was laser-focused on course awareness.

On the first run I had not really registered the turnaround properly, so this
time I was actively hunting for it. I kept looking for the sign, checking the
distance on the watch, and trying not to be the idiot who loses a race because
he simply does not know where he is supposed to go.

That turned out to be the right instinct.

The turnaround came after a blind `90-degree` turn and then a short straight of
roughly `200 m`, after which you turned around and came back through the same
corner. It was not complicated once you knew it was there, but it was exactly
the kind of detail you could miss if you were racing low on energy and oxygen.

Coming back off that left-hand turn, I finally saw Michael again. He was moving
well. I did the rough arithmetic in my head and figured I had about `40`
seconds with something like `1K` to go. At my current pace, somewhere between
`4:10` and `4:30/km`, that felt like enough if I stayed composed.

One of the under-19 athletes I had passed on the bike also came back by me on
the run, but that was irrelevant to my category race, so I let him go.

The important thing was that I kept moving, kept the pace from falling apart,
and got to the line still ahead of Michael.

It was not a particularly fast run by any stretch of the imagination, but at
least it looks like I managed some sort of negative split. Probably the first one of my
running career...

## Results

I crossed the line `3rd` overall and `2nd` in `Men40-49`, which made it four
podiums from four races this season.

[![](https://storage.googleapis.com/blogs_josa/sport/blog_assets/2026-08-29_WASAGA_BEACH_SPRINT_DUATHLON/img/thumbnail/21.jpg)](https://storage.googleapis.com/blogs_josa/sport/blog_assets/2026-08-29_WASAGA_BEACH_SPRINT_DUATHLON/img/full/21.jpg)

That alone would have been a satisfying way to close the year. But the finish
also came with a strange twist.

After I finished, I expected Michael Shay to appear not long afterwards. He had
looked close enough on the run that I assumed the final gap would be well under
a minute.

Instead, he never showed up.

Eventually the results made it clear what had happened: he finished almost
eight minutes behind me. There is no realistic way that gap comes from normal
racing over the final `2.5K`. The only explanation that makes sense is that he
missed the turnaround and ran significantly farther than he should have.

That is rough. It obviously hurt his race, and selfishly it also makes my own
result a bit harder to read because I would have liked a clean head-to-head
finish. Still, that is part of racing too. You have to be fit enough to race
hard, but you also have to pay attention to where the course actually goes.

Looking at the full results afterwards, the race was not especially deep at the
front, but a podium is a podium. Only two athletes in the category broke `1:10`, and I ended
up just under that mark in `1:08:29`.

So I will take it.

It was not a perfect race. The first run was too aggressive, the legs were
never far from cramping, and the course setup had some flaws. But it was also a
proper race effort, a solid result, and a much better way to end the season
than the uncertainty that hung over Barrie.

Here is how my position evolved through the race.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

rankings_progression <- read.csv(
  "analysis_data/all_races.csv",
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
) |>
  filter(ATHLETE == "ADRIAN JOSEPH") |>
  transmute(
    `Run 1 overall` = RANKING_OVERALL_SPORT_1,
    `T1 overall` = RANKING_OVERALL_AFTER_T_1,
    `Bike overall` = RANKING_OVERALL_AFTER_SPORT_2,
    `T2 overall` = RANKING_OVERALL_AFTER_T_2,
    `Run 2 overall` = RANKING_OVERALL,
    `Run 1 category` = RANKING_CATEGORY_SPORT_1,
    `T1 category` = RANKING_CATEGORY_AFTER_T_1,
    `Bike category` = RANKING_CATEGORY_AFTER_SPORT_2,
    `T2 category` = RANKING_CATEGORY_AFTER_T_2,
    `Run 2 category` = RANKING_CATEGORY
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = c("leg", "ranking_type"),
    names_pattern = "^(.*) (overall|category)$",
    values_to = "ranking"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    leg = factor(leg, levels = c("Run 1", "T1", "Bike", "T2", "Run 2")),
    ranking_type = factor(
      ranking_type,
      levels = c("overall", "category"),
      labels = c("Overall ranking", "Category ranking")
    ),
    ranking = as.numeric(ranking)
  )

ranking_limits <- rankings_progression |>
  group_by(ranking_type) |>
  summarise(
    ranking = c(min(ranking, na.rm = TRUE) - 1, max(ranking, na.rm = TRUE) + 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(rankings_progression, aes(x = leg, y = ranking, group = 1)) +
  geom_blank(data = ranking_limits, aes(y = ranking), inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6, color = "#1f4e79") +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "#1f4e79") +
  geom_text(aes(label = ranking), vjust = -0.8, size = 3.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = function(x) {
      seq(floor(min(x, na.rm = TRUE)), ceiling(max(x, na.rm = TRUE)), by = 1)
    },
    labels = function(x) as.integer(x)
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ ranking_type, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Position",
    title = "Ranking progression through the race"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

This chart tells the race in a way that feels much closer to how it actually
unfolded in my head.

The zero line is my race. Anyone below it was up the road from me at that
point. Anyone above it was behind. So what matters is not just where each line
sits, but how it moves from one leg to the next. When a line climbs, I am
bringing that athlete back. When it drops, the gap is opening against me.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

format_min_sec <- function(total_seconds) {
  total_seconds <- round(as.numeric(total_seconds))
  minutes <- total_seconds %/% 60
  seconds <- total_seconds %% 60
  sprintf("%d:%02d", minutes, seconds)
}

all_races <- read.csv(
  "analysis_data/all_races.csv",
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

my_category <- all_races |>
  filter(ATHLETE == "ADRIAN JOSEPH") |>
  pull(CATEGORY)

cumulative_times <- function(data) {
  data |>
    transmute(
      athlete = ATHLETE,
      `Run 1` = as.numeric(RESULT_SPORT_1),
      `T1` = as.numeric(RESULT_SPORT_1) + as.numeric(RESULT_T_1),
      `Bike` = as.numeric(RESULT_SPORT_1) + as.numeric(RESULT_T_1) +
        as.numeric(RESULT_SPORT_2),
      `T2` = as.numeric(RESULT_SPORT_1) + as.numeric(RESULT_T_1) +
        as.numeric(RESULT_SPORT_2) + as.numeric(RESULT_T_2),
      `Run 2` = as.numeric(RESULT_FINAL)
    ) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = c(`Run 1`, `T1`, `Bike`, `T2`, `Run 2`),
      names_to = "leg",
      values_to = "cumulative_time"
    )
}

podium_progression <- bind_rows(
  all_races |>
    filter(as.numeric(RANKING_OVERALL) %in% c(1, 2, 3)) |>
    cumulative_times() |>
    mutate(ranking_type = "Overall ranking"),
  all_races |>
    filter(CATEGORY == my_category, as.numeric(RANKING_CATEGORY) %in% c(1, 2, 3)) |>
    cumulative_times() |>
    mutate(ranking_type = "Category ranking")
) |>
  mutate(athlete = tools::toTitleCase(tolower(athlete))) |>
  mutate(
    ranking_type = factor(
      ranking_type,
      levels = c("Overall ranking", "Category ranking")
    ),
    leg = factor(leg, levels = c("Run 1", "T1", "Bike", "T2", "Run 2"))
  )

gap_to_adrian <- podium_progression |>
  group_by(ranking_type, leg) |>
  mutate(
    adrian_time = cumulative_time[athlete == "Adrian Joseph"][1],
    gap_seconds = cumulative_time - adrian_time
  ) |>
  ungroup()

gap_to_adrian_limits <- gap_to_adrian |>
  group_by(ranking_type) |>
  summarise(
    gap_seconds = c(
      floor(min(gap_seconds, na.rm = TRUE)) - 10,
      ceiling(max(gap_seconds, na.rm = TRUE)) + 10
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  gap_to_adrian,
  aes(x = leg, y = gap_seconds, color = athlete, group = athlete)
) +
  geom_blank(data = gap_to_adrian_limits, aes(y = gap_seconds), inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4, color = "black") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "Mark Danyluk" = "#7f8c8d",
    "Noah Lengyel" = "#d95f02",
    "Adrian Joseph" = "#1f4e79",
    "Michael Shay" = "#4daf4a"
  )) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) {
    prefix <- ifelse(x > 0, "+", "")
    paste0(prefix, format_min_sec(abs(x)))
  }) +
  facet_wrap(~ ranking_type, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Gap to Adrian Joseph",
    title = "Gap to Adrian Joseph by leg",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

## Duathlon series standings

This race mattered a bit beyond the single-day result because it also changed
the `Men40-49` standings in the MultiSport Canada duathlon series.

Coming out of Wasaga, I moved to the top of the category with `265` points from
`3` races. That puts me `10` points ahead of Robert Cardie and `30` ahead of
Michael Shay.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

series_points <- read.csv(
  "analysis_data/final_table_adrian_category.csv",
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(
    category = toupper(category),
    names = tools::toTitleCase(tolower(names)),
    tot_points = as.numeric(tot_points),
    n_races = as.numeric(n_races)
  ) |>
  filter(category == "M40-49") |>
  arrange(desc(tot_points), desc(n_races), names) |>
  transmute(
    Rank = row_number(),
    Athlete = names,
    `Total points` = tot_points,
    `Races counted` = n_races
  )

knitr::kable(series_points |> slice_head(n = 10), align = c("r", "l", "r", "r"))
```

Because I am not doing the final race, my total is locked at `265`. That means
the only question is how many other athletes can still get past that number
with one more score.

The realistic danger comes from three people:

- Robert Cardie needs `3rd` or better.
- Romuald Le Calonnec needs `6th` or better.
- Andrew Roberts needs `1st` or `2nd`; `2nd` would tie me on points, but he
  holds the Barrie tiebreak.

Michael Shay can still pass me too, but only by winning, which looks less
likely on sprint form.

Looking at the previous sprint results, the only really plausible way I fall
off the podium is if Romuald wins, Andrew finishes `2nd`, and Robert finishes
`3rd`. That is the cleanest scenario consistent with the form each of them has
shown this season.

Interestingly, Michael Shay probably helps me more than he hurts me if he shows
up. Unless he wins, he does not pass me in the series, but he could still take
that crucial `3rd` place away from Robert. If that happens, Robert stays behind
me in the standings, and I likely hold on to `3rd`.

## Venue review

I still do not think this is a venue I would choose just for its own sake.

Removing the swim made it much more appealing than the triathlon version, but
there were still some course-design details that felt rough around the edges.
The main one was on the bike, where athletes entering and exiting transition
were sharing the same lane late in the leg. In practice that created something
close to a mandatory no-pass zone with mixed speeds and mixed handling ability,
which felt messy and unnecessarily risky.

Michael was also not the only athlete to miss the turnaround on the final run.
Looking through the results afterwards, I found about a dozen athletes whose
second run was inconsistently longer than half of their first run, which makes
it very likely that the same thing happened to them as well.

It is true that the rules clearly state that athletes are responsible for
knowing the course. That part is not really debatable. Still, I think
MultiSport Canada should consider stationing a volunteer at that turnaround
point. It feels like a simple fix that would avoid the issue altogether.

So my view is more positive than it was two years ago, but only to a point. As
a duathlon, it works well enough. As a polished race venue, I still think there
is room for improvement.
